title: Year Without a Summer
summary: After the April 1815 eruption of Tambora, the summer of 1816 was unusually cold across Europe and northeastern North America, with a June snowstorm in northern New England, July frosts in Maine and failed harvests. Modern assessments attribute at least 100,000 deaths to it, and a 2019 study found volcanic forcing made the European cold up to 100 times more likely in models.

uncertainty.note: The cold summer of 1816; EBSCO dates the New England snowstorm to 7-8 June 1816 and the Tambora eruption to April 1815.

where.modern_name: Northern Hemisphere, chiefly Europe and northeastern North America (no single location)
where.historical_name: Global climate anomaly; affected places included Europe, New England, China and India

importance.justification: A well-documented volcanic climate shock that caused crop failure and famine across several continents.

related.because: Sulfate aerosols from the April 1815 Tambora eruption blocked sunlight and cooled the summer of 1816, according to the sources opened.

sources.title: Disentangling the causes of the 1816 European year without a summer
sources.author: Andrew P. Schurer and others

beats.caption: Tambora erupts in April 1815, and its sulfate aerosols block sunlight.
A snowstorm hits northern New England on 7-8 June 1816, and Europe has a cold, dark, wet summer.
Crop failures send grain and oatmeal prices up, in some cases several-fold, and spark riots in European cities.

reviewer_note: Least sure: the pin is a global placeholder (0,0) because effects were wide with no type site; radii in the animation are visual only. EBSCO notes a concurrent solar lull (Dalton Minimum) and the IOP study finds circulation explains about a quarter of the cooling, so Tambora was not the only factor; the at-least-100,000 deaths figure includes about 11,000 in Indonesia per EBSCO.
